title: From Document Review to Fact Intelligence, Gregory Mostyn on How Wexler.ai Is Reshaping Litigation
author: Gregory Mostyn

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Mostyn does not engage the cluster’s central expertise-reproduction paradox or propose reconstructed apprenticeship. He instead frames automated document review as eliminating dead time and redirecting lawyers toward strategy and client value; the supplied training question receives no substantive answer.
qs: It’s dead time, basically, which we can massively reduce, meaning people can go home earlier.
They can spend more time focusing on strategy and how to actually use this information.

st.t: Neglected claims: AI services target uneconomic legal work
st.an: Mostyn shifts the focus from bounded, low-price services that make neglected claims economical to augmenting lawyers in existing litigation by overcoming document-volume constraints. His proposed benefit is broader evidence review and reduced manual burden, and he offers intended rather than demonstrated outcomes.

And I thought, hang on a minute, we could build something or actually  we can review everything and give it the attention it deserves so that every client gets the best representation.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Mostyn supports the cluster’s view that AI may shift lawyers from document review toward strategy and human advocacy, and he treats adoption claims cautiously. However, he does not address whether removing review work weakens apprenticeship, associate development or partner succession, nor does he propose explicit training or alternative career pathways. His evidence therefore does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal expertise-pipeline proposition.
qs: So yeah, we’re definitely hearing that people are ⁓ massively reducing the kind of busy work and it’s freeing up time to think more strategically.

Gregory Mostyn (29:10)  Yeah, so I think this is I kind of already touched on this, but I think it’s going to be about I think the human side of AI is going to be even more important because the sort of document review side is even less important.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Mostyn accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI will automate bounded production work while increasing the relative value of lawyers. He materially develops it for litigation by arguing that reduced document review redirects effort toward strategy and human advocacy, and that fees should increasingly reflect representation and value rather than review hours. His evidence is anecdotal and he acknowledges early adoption and uncertain wider economics.
qs: So yeah, we’re definitely hearing that people are ⁓ massively reducing the kind of busy work and it’s freeing up time to think more strategically.
Because if Wexler was in a big dispute, I definitely want them to be using AI, but I still want there to be humans there representing my best interest because that’s what you pay for.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Mostyn accepts the cluster’s core copilot model and develops it through a concrete litigation workflow: AI is bounded to supplied evidence, structures facts and contradictions, and redirects lawyers toward strategy and advocacy. He also makes source-level verification, training and change management central, while acknowledging variable output and imperfect accuracy. The contribution is operationally specific, though performance claims are largely vendor-reported rather than independently validated.
qs: So as much as it’s a very helpful digital training, as you say, but it’s limited to the four corners of the page of the documents plus the metadata that you’re giving it.

So  but I think it is highly, highly accurate and more than anything, the verification flow where you can really quickly click on each source and independently verify it is helpful, one, to verify, but two, you’re actually looking at all the documents and you’re getting familiar with the documents as they should be viewed as if they are printed out and you’re finding those patterns too.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between rapid product expansion and demonstrated value: it reports growth in mapped product placements rather than adoption, revenue or performance, while its claims about specialised litigation infrastructure are promotional assertions rather than measured outcomes. Mostyn’s explicitly speculative forecast also supports the cluster’s view that automation may increase the premium on advocacy and contextual judgment.
qs: As of March 2026, we’re right around 1,000 product placements on the map, which is a milestone that we’ve been looking forward to since we launched the first map.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Mostyn supports selective, practical learning over chasing industry noise: he limits broad reading, focuses on customer needs and case-specific training, and treats market-adoption claims cautiously because meaningful use remains early. His position aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on filtering, contextual intelligence and hands-on application, though it rests largely on practitioner experience and customer anecdotes.
qs: But I try not to, I try not to read too much about what’s going on.
I kind of just like I always try and stay focused on what we’re doing and  and just building something that great to our customers.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Mostyn supports the cluster’s core view that AI can reallocate routine legal production toward higher-value, outcome-focused judgment rather than mechanically eliminate billable work. His litigation anecdote also fits the cluster’s caution that current evidence is early and anecdotal, while his forecast that advocacy will become more important aligns with continued reliance on human judgment.
qs: So he wasn’t losing any billable time, but the time that he was billing was much more valuable for the outcome of the case and in the kind of theater of litigation, that’s what you’re looking for on the upper hand.
And so, yes, there’s so much noise and there’s so much hype and there’s so many VC dollars going into this market, but actually I think we’re still very early.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Mostyn supports the cluster’s core proposition through a specialist litigation-review use case: AI can address document-intensive legal work that manual review cannot cover comprehensively. His account also fits the cluster’s evidentiary caution because improved representation and reduced working hours are presented as ambitions, not demonstrated outcomes; it does not establish lawyer–engineer collaboration, human verification, or operational reliability.
qs: They probably physically couldn’t in a lot of cases because there were too many documents to review manually.
And I thought, hang on a minute, we could build something or actually  we can review everything and give it the attention it deserves so that every client gets the best representation.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Mostyn supports the cluster’s view that automation may reallocate legal work toward distinctly human capabilities, especially oral advocacy, storytelling and client-derived context. He also points to intensified advocacy training as an organisational response, while presenting these outcomes as forecasts rather than measured effects.
qs: It’s going to be about the way that you interface your client and the way that you bring the context that’s maybe not written down on any pieces of document, on any document into the story and how you bring it all together.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: Mostyn supports selective augmentation by presenting AI as a tool for reducing low-value factual review and redirecting lawyers’ time toward strategic judgment. His acknowledgment of variable outputs and reliance on a customer anecdote rather than measured results also fit the cluster’s caution that gains are uneven and do not establish broad economic effects, although he does not directly address verification or responsibility.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Mostyn supports the proposition that AI can substitute for document-review tasks while complementing lawyers’ strategic work, without implying wholesale lawyer replacement or a necessary loss of billable work. His customer anecdote illustrates task redistribution and potentially higher-value lawyer time, but he does not establish broader staffing, revenue or employment effects.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of a rapidly expanding but uneven legal-AI market, distinguishing product placements from broader market outcomes and identifying growth in operational, compliance and specialised litigation tools. It also aligns with the cluster’s caution by treating consolidation as a possibility, future expansion as a forecast and Wexler’s performance claims as promotional rather than measured evidence. It does not materially extend the cluster’s disciplined-procurement analysis.

kp.k: Legal AI product placements grow and shift toward operations
kp.d: Stephanie Wilkins reports that the Legal Technology Hub map grew from 400 product placements in February 2025 to about 500 two weeks later, about 850 at the end of 2025, and right around 1,000 in March 2026. These are product-placement counts, although she describes them as market growth. She identifies operations and compliance as the largest recent growth areas and interprets this as a shift toward practical implementation. Her projection of 1500 placements for second quarter 2027 is explicitly speculative.
qs: As of March 2026, we’re right around 1,000 product placements on the map
Our end of the year map for 2025 had about 850 product placements.
this time around we’re seeing our biggest areas of growth in more bread and butter or less trendy areas, if you will, like law firm operations and compliance.
second quarter of 2027? I’ll go 1500.

kp.k: Fact intelligence shifts analysis from documents to events
kp.d: Mostyn presents Wexler's approach as extracting discrete events, assigning relevance using attorney-provided issues, and reasoning over the resulting fact database. He argues that responsive-document retrieval alone is insufficient where language is obscured or accounts conflict. The intended output is a fact-supported litigation narrative rather than merely a relevant document set; this is his account of product design and its value, not a comparative study.
qs: It’s not that helpful to say, here are the documents that are responsive to certain search terms, because people don’t speak in search terms.

the process of basically extracting the discrete observable happenings, if you like, i.e. the events from the documents, assigning relevance based on a list of issues that the attorney themselves provide
You’re not just saying, are some relevant documents. You’re saying, this is what happened and this is why it matters.

kp.k: Specialized analysis complements initial discovery filtering
kp.d: Mostyn positions Wexler as a strategic analysis layer following an initial relevance cull, although it can also support early assessment of client-produced documents. He reports capacity for 250,000 documents and hopes to reach a million by year-end 2026. He cautions against uploading an entire custodian mailbox and identifies deposition preparation, trial preparation, summary judgments, briefing, early case assessment, arbitration and investigations as uses.
qs: We can do 250,000 documents, which is, I think, higher than most of the LLM legal platforms I’ve come across.
we hope to get to a million by the end of the year.
There’s no point putting a whole custodian’s mailbox in Wexler, because you want to know that what you’re putting in is at least broadly relevant to the case
there is that first step, which is critical for the first cull

kp.k: Structured fact pipelines underpin claimed specialization
kp.d: Mostyn attributes differentiation from generalist AI to a 15-step, multi-model pipeline that normalizes messy material into structured facts rather than placing documents into a single context window. He argues that models favor structured information and may otherwise miss contemporaneous evidence. The fact database also supports live deposition fact-checking. He describes the architecture as modular, benefiting from improvements in underlying models.
qs: we pass them through this 15 step pipeline, which doesn’t just stuff documents into one context window
we stitch together all these different models into this 15 step process, which rationalizes and elucidates that complex information, normalizes it into structured data
one of them is real time, which is basically like live fact checking for depositions. And it’s only possible because of that database we built up.
one new model release improves one part of our product and so on and so on.

kp.k: Contradiction detection does not establish external truth
kp.d: Mostyn says the Kim assistant identifies patterns and contradictions only within supplied documents and metadata, without internet searches or reliance on training data for answers. He explicitly disclaims judging veracity beyond that universe. The proposed role is augmentation: lawyers retain responsibility for applying law, researching externally and understanding the case, rather than relying solely on what AI reports.
qs: We don’t opine on the veracity of things, right? We only look at the documents that we’ve been given.
if it’s not contradicted by another piece of data within the same data set, that’s not our job.
It should be like an accelerant and enhancement.
you actually know what’s going on, not just the AIs told me this.

kp.k: Accuracy claims remain qualified and require human verification
kp.d: Mostyn initially claims the restricted approach can 'basically eliminate' hallucination risk, but later explicitly rejects 100 % accuracy. He cites structured data, restrictive instructions, sentence-level sourcing and quick human source verification as safeguards, and reports customer comparisons with generalist platforms without presenting protocols or results. The 95 % accuracy and 90 % junior-review-time savings figures appear in Gebauer's question, not as demonstrated findings or figures independently substantiated by Mostyn.
qs: This is how we minimize, basically eliminate hallucination risk, inaccuracies, those kind of things.
everything is sourced down not just to the document but to the sentence that it’s been taken from.
Can we say it’s 100 % accurate? Of course not.
the verification flow where you can really quickly click on each source and independently verify it is helpful

kp.k: Review automation reallocates time toward litigation strategy
kp.d: Mostyn argues that AI reduces unvaluable or unbilled review time, improves working hours and frees lawyers for strategic analysis. He relays a partner customer's estimate that finding an inconsistency manually might have taken a couple of days; the partner instead used that time for strategy without losing billable time. He also reports an inconsistency missed by a forensic accountant and describes adversarial rehearsal with the assistant. These are vendor-carried customer anecdotes, not quantified productivity findings.

kp.k: Pricing may move toward outcomes and representative assurance
kp.d: Mostyn reports seeing fixed fees, value-based billing interest and hybrid project-based arrangements among some customers. He argues that high-stakes clients buy human representation and assurance rather than document-review hours, and recommends longer-term movement toward value-based pricing. He distinguishes this prospective economic change from near-term reduction of wasted time rather than predicting immediate elimination of hourly billing.
qs: Increasingly, we are seeing fixed fees with some of our clients, people looking for more kind of value based billing or maybe like a hybrid
the value system should be reflective more of that rather than just the number of hours of documents that you’re reviewing.

longer term, I think we need to start thinking more about kind of value based.

kp.d: Mostyn explains that Wexler charges by consumption rather than seats, allowing access for law-firm clients and independent UK barristers. He says end-client feedback is indirect and reports appreciation for value and review coverage. His comparison with fatigued human reviewers is an argument for AI-assisted coverage, not measured evidence that every relevant fact is found.

kp.k: Adoption requires practical training and general AI literacy
kp.d: Mostyn describes hands-on sub-practice-group training, matter-specific top-ups and general AI workshops. He emphasizes explaining why sophisticated reasoning capabilities coexist with elementary failures and why outputs vary. Source verification is also presented as a way for lawyers to become familiar with case documents. Separately, his conversations with practicing lawyers lead him to characterize actual adoption as early despite licenses, experimentation and market hype.

kp.k: Automation could increase the importance of oral advocacy
kp.d: Asked about the next three to five years, Mostyn predicts that document review and fact-finding will be largely automated within a few years, making argument delivery, storytelling, client interaction and unwritten context more important. His hypothetical assumes previously undiscovered evidence becomes harder to find because comprehensive review is available. He expects AI-assisted advocacy preparation to grow in value and likens lawyers' preparation to athletic training; this is a forecast rather than an observed professional restructuring.

lawyers are going to want to train up for those kind of things just as athletes preparing for the big race

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mostyn argues that specialised AI turns litigation documents into structured factual intelligence, accelerates factual analysis and shifts lawyers’ work toward strategy and advocacy. Wilkins separately describes growth and maturation in the legal-AI product market.
pts.d: Mostyn describes Wexler’s 15-step extraction pipeline as normalising messy documents into discrete events, with relevance assigned against lawyer-supplied issues. He positions this as complementary to eDiscovery rather than a replacement for its initial filtering function. The resulting fact bank supports case analysis, adversarial preparation and live identification of contradictions in deposition testimony. He claims that structured data, restricted sourcing and sentence-level citations improve accuracy relative to generalist tools. He describes substantial potential time savings, including an illustrative reduction from weeks or days to hours, and says customers redirect effort from document processing toward strategy. He does not predict an immediate disappearance of billable work: his partner example retains billable time while making it more valuable. He reports some customers adopting fixed fees or hybrid arrangements and anticipates further movement toward value-based pricing. Over the next few years, he predicts largely automated document review and fact-finding will increase the importance of human oral advocacy, contextual understanding and client relationships. Separately, Wilkins reports almost 1,000 legal-AI product placements in March 2026, compared with approximately 500 around Legal Week 2025, and says growth is shifting toward operations and compliance. These are product-placement counts, not independently established measures of market revenue or adoption. She forecasts 1,500 placements in Q2 2027.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Mostyn relies on founder experience, customer conversations, reported customer comparisons and illustrative case anecdotes; Wilkins supplies counts from successive legal-tech maps.
pts.d: Mostyn grounds the product’s rationale in observing intensive manual review in his legal family, early prototype testing with family members and conversations with hundreds of people across the UK and US. For comparative accuracy, he reports customers regularly testing Wexler against generalist platforms, but supplies no test design, sample size, measured error rate or named benchmark. The technical explanation—structured extraction, restricted document scope, sentence-level sourcing and source-checking workflows—is offered as a basis for improved reliability. His efficiency and strategy claims draw on customer anecdotes: a partner allegedly found an inconsistency sooner and used the saved time for strategy; another customer found an inconsistency a forensic accountant had missed. He characterises such feedback as recurrent, without providing a systematic study. End-client reactions are explicitly indirect. The interview does not establish Mostyn’s own measured 95% accuracy or 90% time-saving result: those figures appear in a host’s question and are not independently substantiated in his answer. Wilkins’s evidence is the Legal Technology Hub map series: 400 placements in February 2025, about 500 two weeks later, about 850 at year-end 2025 and approximately 1,000 in March 2026. Her interpretation that conversations are maturing also draws on Legal Week observations. The advocacy and pricing forecasts are Mostyn’s expectations rather than demonstrated future outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Present capabilities are bounded by the supplied document set and human checking; greater processing scale is a 2026 aspiration, while substantial automation and advocacy changes are forecasts for the next several years.
pts.d: At the time of the 2026 interview, Mostyn says Wexler can process 250,000 documents and hopes to reach one million by year-end. He conditions its use on a broadly relevant document universe, often following an initial eDiscovery cull; the claim to review everything therefore concerns the material supplied for analysis, not necessarily every document associated with a dispute. The system identifies contradictions within supplied documents and metadata, rather than establishing external truth, searching the internet or conducting independent case-law research. Although he initially describes hallucination risk as essentially eliminated, he later expressly disclaims 100% accuracy, acknowledges output variability and emphasises human verification and training. His immediate economic expectation is less wasted time and more strategic work; value-based pricing is a longer-term direction without a firm deadline. His prediction of largely automated review and fact-finding answers a question about the next three to five years and is expressed as occurring within a few years. The proposed shift toward advocacy assumes factual discovery becomes much more comprehensive. He also says actual lawyer penetration remains low and adoption is still early. Wilkins’s market observations cover February 2025 to March 2026; her 1,500-placement forecast concerns Q2 2027. She acknowledges consolidation might eventually shrink the map but says current observations do not show that happening.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are litigation teams, trial advocates and their clients, with additional implications for legal innovation teams and operations and compliance product markets.
pts.d: Mostyn identifies deposition preparation, trial preparation, summary judgments, briefing and early case assessment as current uses, and extends the scope to arbitration and investigations across jurisdictions. Lawyers doing intensive document review may spend less time on manual processing and more on strategy, preparation and understanding the factual record. He predicts greater pressure on advocates’ performance in mediation, arbitration, depositions and trial as factual analysis becomes more automated. His framing is augmentation: humans continue to check sources, apply law, represent clients and supply context absent from documents. He anticipates improved quality of life for litigators and better value and outcomes for clients, without supplying quantified end-client outcomes or projecting particular staffing reductions. Consumption-based rather than seat-based pricing allows clients and independent UK barristers to access the same platform. Practice groups and lawyers require hands-on training, matter-specific support and general education about generative AI’s limitations. Wilkins’s observations concern the legal-tech supplier landscape and firms’ internal operations and compliance functions; they do not establish effects on unmet civil legal need.
